text: The caravela-portuguesa (Portuguese man o' war) that washes up on southern Brazilian beaches in winter and spring isn't a jellyfish at all — it's a siphonophore, a colony of specialised individuals living as one animal under a gas-filled float. Its tentacles can sting for hours after the animal is dead on the sand, so never touch one, even dry.

Southern right whales (baleia-franca) come to the shallow bays of Santa Catarina's south coast every winter to calve, often within a few hundred metres of the beach. The stretch from Florianópolis south to Balneário Rincão is a federal protected area for them, and the season runs roughly June to November.

Humpback whales (baleia-jubarte) travel up the Brazilian coast from Antarctic feeding grounds to breed in warmer water, passing Santa Catarina between about July and November. Calm mornings with little wind are when a blow or a breach is easiest to spot from shore.

Green turtles (tartaruga-verde) are the vegetarians of the sea-turtle family: adults graze on seagrass and algae, and juveniles feed year-round around rocky points along the southern Brazilian coast. If you see one surface for a breath while you swim, keep your distance and let it be.

Sea foam is mostly whipped-up organic matter — proteins, lipids and the remains of algal blooms — churned by waves like the froth on a cappuccino. On its own it isn't pollution, but a persistent brown, smelly foam at a stream mouth is worth reporting.

On the southern Brazilian coast the water can turn suddenly colder in the middle of summer: persistent north-easterly winds push the warm surface layer offshore and cold, nutrient-rich water rises from below to replace it. That upwelling is why a January swim can feel like July.

The ocean has absorbed roughly a quarter to a third of the carbon dioxide humans have emitted since the industrial revolution, and it is measurably more acidic as a result — surface seawater pH has dropped by about 0.1, a 30% increase in acidity.

Below about 200 metres no sunlight reaches, yet the deep sea is far from dark: most animals living there make their own light. Bioluminescence is the rule rather than the exception in the largest habitat on Earth.
